title: CORS Policies and Named Policies in ASP.NET Core
description: Define reusable CORS policies and apply them globally, per controller, or per action.

data.text: Inline policies work for small demos, but real applications usually need different rules for different parts of the API. A public API might allow any origin, while an admin area should only accept requests from trusted internal domains. Named policies let you define each rule once and reuse it everywhere.

data.title: Keep Policies Centralized
data.text: Define all CORS policies in Program.cs so you can audit and update them in one place instead of hunting through controllers.
Call AddPolicy inside AddCors to create a named policy. The name is just a string key you will reference later.

data.title: Program.cs — Named Policy Definition
data.content: Register a named CORS policy called 'AdminPolicy' that only allows trusted origins.

data.caption: How a named CORS policy flows from registration to request
data.definition:
flowchart LR
    A[AddCors AddPolicy] --> B[Named policy stored in DI]
    B --> C[UseCors applies middleware]
    C --> D{Request arrives}
    D -->|Matching controller/action| E[EnableCors attribute selects policy]
    D -->|No attribute| F[Global UseCors policy applies]
    E --> G[CORS headers added to response]
    F --> G

data.text: Use the EnableCors attribute on a controller class. Every action in that controller inherits the same policy unless an action overrides it.

data.title: Controller-Level CORS Policy
data.content: Apply the 'PublicApi' policy to all actions in a controller.

data.text: Place the attribute directly on an action method. The action policy overrides the controller policy for that single method.

data.title: Action-Level CORS Policy
data.content: Override the controller policy for a single sensitive action.

data.text: Disabling CORS for a Controller or Action
Use DisableCors when you want to block cross-origin access for a specific endpoint even if a global or controller-level policy exists.

data.title: Disabling CORS on an Action
data.content: Block all cross-origin access to a specific action.

data.text: If your policy calls AllowCredentials(), you cannot also call AllowAnyOrigin(). The browser will reject the response because allowing credentials from every origin is unsafe. Always pair AllowCredentials with WithOrigins and explicit domain names.

data.title: Common Mistake
data.text: Calling AllowAnyOrigin() together with AllowCredentials() causes a runtime CORS error. Use WithOrigins("https://example.com") instead when credentials are required.

data.title: Create a Named Policy
data.description: Practice defining and applying a named CORS policy in a new ASP.NET Core Web API project.
steps: Create a new Web API project.
Register a named policy called 'MobileApp' that allows https://mobile.example.com.
Add a second policy called 'InternalTools' that allows https://tools.example.com and requires credentials.
Verify the project builds without errors.
data.expectedOutcome: You should have two named CORS policies registered and applied at the controller level.

items.text: I can define a named CORS policy with AddPolicy
I know how to apply a policy at the controller level
I can override the controller policy on a single action
I understand why AllowCredentials and AllowAnyOrigin cannot be combined
I can use DisableCors to block cross-origin access for an endpoint

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Named policies centralize CORS rules and make them reusable
Use EnableCors on controllers or actions to apply a named policy
Use DisableCors to explicitly block cross-origin access
AllowCredentials requires explicit origins, not AllowAnyOrigin
data.takeaway: Next, you will learn how CORS preflight requests work and how ASP.NET Core handles them.
